Connecticut Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Connecticut house?

Check the statute and talk to a Connecticut attorney about your facts.

How long must someone occupy land in Connecticut to claim it?

The statute that governs this is a fifteen-year limit on the owner's right to enter. Section 52-575(a) says no person may make entry into lands except within fifteen years after the right or title first accrues, or within fifteen years after being ousted from possession.

The statute speaks from the owner's side. It tells an owner how long the right to take back the land lasts, and what the owner can do to stop the clock. The statute text gives the time limit and does not list the other elements an occupant would have to prove, so an attorney's read of your facts matters more than any short summary.

Fifteen years is the number to remember. Nothing in section 52-575 shortens it for an occupant who has been in the house a short time.

How can an owner interrupt the clock?

An owner can serve a written notice and record it, then file suit within one year. Section 52-575(a) says that entry is not sufficient unless, within the fifteen-year period, a person claiming ownership gives written notice to the persons in possession that they dispute the right of possession and want to prevent the other party from acquiring the right.

The notice must be served and recorded as provided in sections 47-39 and 47-40, and it counts as an interruption of use and possession. The owner then has to commence an action within one year after the notice is recorded.

  • Write a notice that says you dispute the right of possession.
  • Serve it like an original summons, as section 47-39 directs.
  • Record it on the land records in the town where the land lies.
  • Start the court action within one year after recording.

Section 47-39, which section 52-575 points to, says the notice is served like an original summons. For a person outside the state it allows service on a tenant or occupant of the estate, or failing that, affixing a copy to the house or another conspicuous part of the premises. Section 47-40 covers the case where the party is unknown. Service rules are technical, so have a lawyer review the paperwork.

Do the time limits stop for minors, people in prison or people who lack capacity?

Yes, in a limited way. Under section 52-575(b), a person who has a right of entry but is a minor, non compos mentis or imprisoned when the right first accrues, and the person's heirs, may enter and serve and record notice within five years after reaching full age, regaining sound mind or being released.

This matters in family-owned houses. An inherited property with an heir who was a child when the owner died, or a co-owner who spent years incarcerated, may have a longer window than the fifteen-year headline suggests. The statute also says the limitation does not begin to run against an owner of a remainder or reversionary interest until the preceding particular estate ends.

A practical result: when a house has a complicated ownership history, do not assume the clock has run out against the owner. Pull the chain of title and ask a lawyer to read it.

What if someone is living in my house and I did not rent to them?

The summary process statute covers this directly. Section 47a-23 allows the owner to serve a notice to quit when the premises are occupied by one who never had a right or privilege to occupy them, and also when someone originally had that right but it has since ended.

The notice to quit must be given at least three days before the time stated in the notice for the occupant to leave, and it must be in writing in the form the statute supplies. If the occupant stays, the next step is a summary process case in court, not changing locks or removing belongings.

SituationStatute that frames it
Occupant never had any right to be there47a-23(a)(2), notice to quit
Right to occupy existed but ended47a-23(a)(3), notice to quit
Lease ended or rent not paid47a-23(a)(1), notice to quit
Owner wants to stop an adverse claim running52-575(a), notice served and recorded, suit within one year

What is the difference between a squatter and a tenant?

A tenant entered under a rental agreement or lease, written or oral, and a squatter did not. That distinction decides which part of section 47a-23 applies. Item (1) of the statute deals with leases and rental agreements that end by lapse of time, by an expressed stipulation, for violation, or for nonpayment of rent. Items (2) and (3) deal with occupants who never had a right or whose right has ended.

An owner who is unsure which one applies should find out before writing a notice. Someone who has been paying rent in cash, or a relative who stayed on after a death, may be treated differently than a stranger who broke in. Text messages, receipts and a written history help. The page on Connecticut landlord and tenant law covers rental occupants in more detail.

Does a recorded deed affect a squatter's claim?

Recording a deed is separate from the notice that interrupts an adverse claim. Section 47-10 provides that a conveyance is not effectual against anyone but the grantor and heirs unless recorded in the town where the land lies, so a buyer should always record. Beyond that, the interruption method is the recorded notice described in section 52-575(a).

Connecticut has 169 municipalities, and each has its own land records. Owners of vacant property can visit it regularly and keep dated photographs of the condition and any signs of occupancy.

Can I sell a house that has an occupant who will not leave?

Yes, though it limits who will buy. Buyers who need a mortgage may struggle to close on a house with a disputed occupant, because possession on the closing date is uncertain. Investors who buy as-is sometimes can, but the occupancy question will affect the price and the timing, and an attorney should review any contract that depends on the occupant's departure.

Before listing, gather what you can: the deed, tax bills, any notice to quit and proof of service, and a note of when you last had the property under your control. That file speeds up a title search and shows a buyer what remains to be done.

What should owners of vacant or inherited Connecticut property keep on file?

Keep a short paper trail, because every deadline in this area runs from a date you may later need to prove. The statutes cited on this page refer to recording, service and filing, so each of those leaves a record.

  • The recorded deed, with the town clerk's recording information.
  • Any notice served under section 52-575, with the proof of service and the recording receipt.
  • The date a notice to quit was given under section 47a-23, and the date stated in it.
  • Dated photographs of the property, taken on each visit.
  • Property tax bills, since they show who the town treats as owner.

With 169 municipalities each keeping its own land records, the clerk in the town where the house sits is the right office to ask about what is recorded against it.

More questions about Connecticut Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

Can a squatter take ownership of a Connecticut house?

Only if every requirement of adverse possession is met for the full period. Section 52-575 sets a fifteen-year limit on the owner's right to enter, and an attorney should assess the facts.

How many years does adverse possession take in Connecticut?

Fifteen years is the period in section 52-575(a). Longer periods can apply when the owner was a minor, of unsound mind or imprisoned when the right first accrued.

How do I stop someone from claiming my land?

Serve written notice disputing their right of possession, record it as sections 47-39 and 47-40 direct, and begin an action within one year after recording.

What notice do I give someone who never had permission to stay?

A written notice to quit under section 47a-23, given at least three days before the date stated for the occupant to leave. If they stay, a summary process action follows.

Can I change the locks on an occupant?

The statutes cited here lay out a notice to quit and a court process. Talk to a Connecticut attorney before using any self-help.

Can I sell my house while a squatter is inside?

You can, but financed buyers may struggle to close. An as-is cash buyer may, and the occupancy affects price and timing.

Which Connecticut laws set the rules between landlords and tenants?

Most of them sit in Title 47a of the General Statutes, which the legislature splits into chapters by subject. A landlord who plans to sell a rental will touch several chapters, so it helps to know which one answers which question.

ChapterSubject
830Rights and responsibilities of landlord and tenant
831Security deposits
832Summary process (eviction)
833Entry and detainer
833aPublic enforcement of health and safety standards in rented dwellings

The Connecticut Judicial Branch law library keeps a landlord and tenant page that links to these chapters, to forms, and to research reports from the Office of Legislative Research. It is a starting point for research, as the page itself says, and not legal advice.

What must a Connecticut landlord keep in working order?

Section 47a-7 requires a landlord to follow the building and housing codes that affect health and safety, and to keep the premises fit and habitable. The duty has exceptions where the tenant or a guest made the place unfit on purpose.

The list in the statute is practical.

  • Make repairs and do whatever is needed to keep the premises fit and habitable.
  • Keep the common areas clean and safe.
  • Maintain electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating and ventilating facilities, appliances and elevators that the landlord supplies or is required to supply, in good and safe working order.
  • Provide and maintain receptacles for ashes, garbage and other waste.

For a seller, these duties follow the house. A buyer who steps into the landlord's role takes on the same obligations, and an inspection that finds worn heating or plumbing in a rented unit can lower a buyer's offer. A buyer of an as-is investment property usually prices that risk in rather than asking for repairs.

When is rent late, and what can a landlord charge?

A tenant has a nine-day grace period after rent is due, and four days for a one-week tenancy. Only after that may a landlord terminate the rental agreement for nonpayment under sections 47a-23 to 47a-23b. The rule is in section 47a-15a.

If the lease has a valid written late-charge agreement, the landlord may charge a fee on a payment made after the grace period. The fee may not exceed the lesser of five dollars a day, up to a maximum of fifty dollars, or five percent of the late payment. Where a government or charitable entity pays part of the rent, the five percent applies to the tenant's share. A landlord may not charge more than one late fee on a single late payment, however long it stays unpaid.

When you sell, a buyer will ask for a rent roll and payment history. Accurate records of due dates, grace periods and any late fees save questions at closing.

Can a landlord show a rented home to buyers?

Yes, with limits. Section 47a-16 says a tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to enter to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, along with entering to inspect or make repairs.

The same section keeps the tenant's privacy intact. A landlord may enter without consent in an emergency, as section 47a-16a permits, under a court order, or if the tenant has abandoned the premises. A landlord may not abuse the right of entry or use it to harass a tenant, and may enter only at reasonable times except in an emergency.

Showings in a rental are easier when the owner plans them with the tenant. Offering set windows, and keeping a short list of who is visiting, usually works better than repeated requests. A cash buyer who wants to view a tenant-occupied house can do a single visit instead of a series of open houses.

What happens to the tenant's security deposit when the landlord sells?

The deposit passes to the new owner. Under section 47a-21, any voluntary or involuntary transfer of a landlord's interest in residential real property to a successor is an assignment to that successor of the landlord's security interest in all deposits paid by the tenants.

The seller also has a duty to move the money. When real estate is transferred from a landlord, other than a receiver, to a successor, the landlord must withdraw the full amount of the deposits, with accrued interest, from the escrow account and deliver it to the successor. If the account holds deposits for other properties and has less than the total owed, the seller delivers a pro rata share for the property being sold.

The word successor in the chapter includes a person who gets the landlord's interest by purchase, foreclosure or otherwise. That is why the chapter treats a buyer as a landlord for deposit purposes.

  • Return deadline: not later than twenty-one days after the tenancy ends, or fifteen days after the tenant gives a written forwarding address, whichever is later.
  • What is returned: the full deposit plus accrued interest, less any damage deductions the landlord is allowed to take.

What must a new owner tell the tenants after closing?

Section 47a-6 puts a duty on the landlord, or a successor landlord, to tell the tenant in writing, at the time of succession, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises. The statute names a second person as well, so read the full text.

The Department of Housing posts mandatory landlord and tenant forms and notice forms on its website, and the Judicial Branch page links them. A buyer who takes over a rental should have the notice ready for closing day, along with the lease copies, the deposit transfer and any records on repairs or complaints.

Tenants do better when the owner tells them about a sale directly. A short written note that names the seller, the buyer and the new contact reduces confusion and missed rent.

Which tenants have extra protection from eviction?

Section 47a-23c limits evictions of older and disabled tenants in larger properties. It applies in a building or complex of five or more dwelling units, or in a mobile manufactured home park, to a tenant who is 62 or older or has a qualifying disability, along with some tenants who live with a relative who meets those conditions.

For those tenants a landlord may sue only on the grounds the statute lists, and a rent increase must be fair and equitable under the criteria in section 7-148c. A protected tenant who is aggrieved by a proposed increase may file with the fair rent commission in the town, if there is one, or go to Superior Court if there is none. The Judicial Branch page also lists Public Act 22-30, an act concerning fair rent commissions effective October 1, 2022.

A sale of the building is not one of the grounds. Buyers of small apartment buildings should ask for the age and status of each tenant before they agree on a price.

What should a Connecticut landlord do before selling a rental?

Gather the paper trail first. A short list will keep the sale on schedule.

  1. Copy each lease and any rental agreement, with rent amounts and dates.
  2. Confirm where each security deposit is held and how much interest has accrued.
  3. Write down repair requests and what was done under section 47a-7.
  4. Check whether any tenant falls under section 47a-23c.
  5. Decide whether to sell with tenants in place or after they leave, and put any move-out agreement in writing.

Selling to a cash investor is common for landlords with tired rentals. The buyer takes the property as-is and handles the leases after closing, so the owner does not need to make repairs, hold showings or wait for a mortgage approval.

More questions about Connecticut Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

What is the maximum security deposit in Connecticut?

The cap is two months' rent for a tenant under 62 and one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older under section 47a-21.

How soon must a landlord return a deposit?

A landlord must deliver the deposit with accrued interest, less allowed deductions, not later than 21 days after the tenancy ends or 15 days after a written forwarding address, whichever is later.

Does a new owner have to honor the existing lease?

The chapter treats a successor as a landlord and passes the deposits to the successor. Whether a lease continues depends on its terms and on the notice and court rules, so read the lease and ask an attorney.

Can a landlord enter a rental without notice?

Only in an emergency, under a court order, as permitted by section 47a-16a, or when the unit has been abandoned. Otherwise entry needs the tenant's consent and a reasonable time.

Where can I find Connecticut landlord and tenant forms?

The Judicial Branch law library page for landlord and tenant law links housing forms, and the Department of Housing posts mandatory notice forms and a model lease.
